extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of The Spectator; readers interested in manners, satire, and social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles embedded in Addison/Steele Spectator essays about composing occasional satirical pieces on manners, fashions, spectacles, and gender — how to criticize without grossing into prejudice, and what to observe and record for posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid general charges against whole bodies of men
rubrics_metrics.description: General Charges against Bodies of Men is the Fault I am writing against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be carried by prejudices into believing that the whole Body of the adverse Party are a Band of Villains and Dæmons; avoid sweeping denunciations of groups (nations, parties, professions) and the 'trifling and superficial' prating that accompanies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject irrational contempt for other nations and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Our common People, and most who have not travelled, have an irrational Contempt for the Language, Dress, Customs, and even the Shape and Minds of other Nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid nationalistic or parochial scorn; recognize that useful talents and genius can arise from unexpected places (e.g., Ireland, Lapland). Satirical writing should not rely on or promote ignorant contempt for foreign ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not satirize entire sexes or broad social classes indiscriminately
rubrics_metrics.description: I always hated Satyrs against Woman, and Satyrs against Man; I am apt to suspect a Stranger who laughs at the Religion of The Faculty; My Spleen rises at a dull Rogue, who is severe upon Mayors and Aldermen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cheap blanket satire targeted at 'women' or 'men' or large professional groups; such broad attacks are unjust and weaken the moral force of satire. Prefer particular targets or behaviours to wholesale denunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect varied talents and show compassion for deficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Necessities of Mankind require various Employments; and whoever excels in his Province is worthy of Praise. All Men are not educated after the same Manner, nor have all the same Talents. Those who are deficient deserve our Compassion, and have a Title to our Assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise excellence in its proper sphere; when noting faults recognize different educations and talents and recommend compassion and assistance rather than mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid instilling vain fraternity-pride by debasing others
rubrics_metrics.description: To swell young Minds with vain Thoughts of the Dignity of their own Brotherhood, by debasing and villifying all others, doth them a real Injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When instructing or praising a cohort (college, society, guild), do not build its self-regard by denigrating outsiders; instead exhibit examples from less celebrated sources to spur honest emulation and wider perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gentle methods to correct social extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: For my own part, I am for treating the Sex with greater Tenderness, and have all along made use of the most gentle Methods to bring them off from any little Extravagance into which they are sometimes unwarily fallen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical correction should aim for gentle persuasion and admonition rather than harsh ridicule, especially when addressing 'little' vanities or feminine irregularities — tenderness is a preferred tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice small encroachments on social boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: I think it however absolutely necessary to keep up the Partition between the two Sexes, and to take Notice of the smallest Encroachments which the one makes upon the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to gradual or novel shifts in custom (e.g., women adopting male dress); record and critique small changes as indicators of larger social trends — the writer's role is vigilance as well as judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and lampoon contemporary fashions and follies (occasional papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another sort of Speculations, which I consider as Occasional Papers, that take their Rise from the Folly, Extravagance, and Caprice of the present Age. For I look upon my self as one set to watch the Manners and Behaviour of my Countrymen and Contemporaries, and to mark down every absurd Fashion, ridiculous Custom, or affected Form of Speech that makes its Appearance in the World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely, occasional essays should record and critique transient customs and fashions; part of the value is contemporaneous exposure of follies, and such pieces also preserve those fashions for posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve accounts of fleeting customs for posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: By this Means I have so effectually quashed those Irregularities which gave Occasion to 'em, that I am afraid Posterity will scarce have a sufficient Idea of them... when I think on the Figure my several Volumes of Speculations will make about a Hundred Years hence, I consider them as so many Pieces of old Plate, where the Weight will be regarded, but the Fashion lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that once corrected, fashions disappear; one duty of the occasional essayist is archival — to leave accurate records of past follies even if their form later seems absurd to future readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame public spectacles with gallantry and honorable motives, not mere brutality
rubrics_metrics.description: We have retained the Barbarity, but lost the Gallantry of the old Combatants... This would give the Battel quite another Turn; and a proper Station for the Ladies... would animate the Disputants with a more gallant Incentive than the Expectation of Money from the Spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing or critiquing violent public entertainments (gladiatorial or combative spectacles), emphasize noble motives (love, honour) rather than spectacle for profit; suggest reforms that restore gallantry and moral framing to otherwise brutal entertainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question the morality of spectatorship — are we delighting in cruelty or pity?
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something in Nature very unaccountable on such Occasions, when we see the People take a certain painful Gratification in beholding these Encounters. Is it Cruelty that administers this Sort of Delight? Or is it a Pleasure which is taken in the Exercise of Pity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire to probe the audience's motives and the ethics of public amusements; call attention to the uncomfortable mix of cruelty and pity in popular entertainments and encourage moral reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe how mutual intercourse between sexes civilizes and produces arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Campaigns which both Sexes passed together made them so well acquainted with one another, that at the End of the War they did not care for parting... As the two Armies romped on these Occasions, the Women complained of the thick bushy Beards... the Men took care to prune themselves... After a few Years conversing together, the Women had learnt to Smile, and the Men to Ogle, the Women grew Soft, and the Men Lively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commenting on social change, note how reciprocal influence between groups can refine manners, invent arts, and produce new social practices; emphasize social interplay rather than one-sided imitation.
